title: Emergency patch coordination and postmortem notes
body:
Summary:

This doc captures the coordination notes, change manifest, canary rollout plan, and a short postmortem for the emergency patch applied to the serving runtime on 2026-03-08 (incident window ~07:12-09:05 UTC). The immediate user impact was increased 95th/99th latency and occasional OOMs under the new batching kernel when sequence length > 4096.

Timeline (high level):
- 2026-03-08 07:10 UTC: Pager alerts (SLO breach) — spike in 95p latency for hosted-api-prod-eu.
- 07:18 UTC: Initial triage in #incident-release. Identified correlation with new kernel rollout (kernel v1.4.7) applied at 04:00 UTC.
- 07:30 UTC: Canary rollback to kernel v1.4.6 on canary pool reduced errors. Decision: isolate runtime build and prepare hotfix.
- 08:05 UTC: Hotfix build (runtime-kernel v1.4.7-hotfix1) created with guard on large sequence batching path (explicitly disable new fusion when seq_len > 2048).
- 08:40 UTC: Coordinated canary rollout (see plan below).
- 09:05 UTC: Canary looks good; gradual ramp to 100% completed by 11:40 UTC with close monitoring.

Root cause hypothesis (confirmed by post-deploy debugging):
- A fusion optimization in kernel v1.4.7 introduced aggressive memory pre-allocation for continuous batching in the large seq_len code path. Under certain request size distributions (seen in EU region), this caused KV-cache misses to allocate beyond reserved pool and hit OOM heuristics, triggering GC/evictions and increased tail latency.
- Regression not caught in previous perf tests because our synthetic workload used uniform sequence lengths; the real traffic had a heavy tail of long sequences from a small set of customers.

Change manifest (hotfix build contents):
- runtime/kernel: v1.4.7 -> v1.4.7-hotfix1 (guard: disable fusion for seq_len > 2048)
- runtime/batching: add additional soft limits and logging around pre-alloc (temp flag hotfix.batch_guard=true)
- infra/autoscaler: tighten fallback policy to drop lower-tier requests if memory pressure detected (temporary until full fix)
- ops/scripts: healthcheck update to include kv-cache eviction rate and mem-reserve headroom metric

Canary rollout plan executed:
- Step 0: Canary pool snapshot and rollback playbook verified (08:10)
- Step 1: 0 -> 1% (08:45) watch 10m for OOM/eviction spikes
- Step 2: 1% -> 5% (09:05) watch 15m, expand traces for affected request ids
- Step 3: 5% -> 25% (09:35) validate latency and error budgets per customer segment
- Step 4: 25% -> 100% (09:50 -> 11:40) gradual final ramp, removed temporary fallback at end
- Rollback triggers: >3 OOMs/min, increase in eviction_rate > 150% baseline, or 99th latency > SLO delta of +80ms for 3 consecutive windows

Observations during rollout:
- Canary at 5% reduced OOM events to near-zero; eviction_rate dropped by ~85% in the canary pool vs pre-fix.
- Two customers with extreme long-sequence workloads still showed higher 99p latency; flagged them for targeted mitigations (see action items).

Postmortem — quick notes:
- What went well:
  - Rapid detection and correlation to kernel roll; good signal routing in dashboards helped narrow to batching kernel.
  - Canary rollback was quick and reduced blast radius while we built hotfix.
  - Cross-team coordination (SRE, Serving Runtime, Release Eng, Customer Success) was effective; on-call handover was clear.
- What went less well:
  - Perf test coverage gap: our pre-release perf harness did not exercise heavy-tail sequence distributions.
  - Telemetry gap: missing a direct metric for "fusion pre-alloc size" made root cause analysis slower.
  - Rollout docs: some engineers were unsure which infra flags were safe to toggle in emergencies (doc pointers inconsistent).

Action items (owner — due):
- Add long-tail seq_len profiles to perf regression suite; include customers X/Y traces (Arjun Patel — 2026-03-20).
- Implement a telemetry gauge for dk_fusion_prealloc_bytes and instrument logging (Samir Gupta — 2026-03-15).
- Consolidate emergency runbook for kernel rollbacks and flag usage (Maya Chen + Lina Romero — 2026-03-14).
- Outreach to two affected customers to discuss traffic shaping and offer mitigations (Dana Lee — 2026-03-12, already started).
- Post-release: remove temporary autoscaler fallback after full fix validated (Release Eng regular ticket) (Arjun Patel — 2026-03-22).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should we change canary percentage cadence for kernel-level rollouts by default (faster or slower)? pros/cons for 1/5/25/100 pattern.
- How do we prioritize adding more realistic traces to our perf lab vs. synthetic scenario generation?

Misc notes and links:
- Incident Slack thread: #incident-release (link pinned to confluence)
- Full debug trace bundle: s3://redwood-debug/2026-03-08/kernel-incident-07-20.tar.gz
- Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/release-engineering/pull/987 (hotfix build and canary scripts)
- Jira: JIRA-RELE-4521 (incident), JIRA-RELE-4522 (perf test backlog item)

Standup log (brief, raw):
- 2026-03-09 10:00 — Maya: roundup; hotfix merged, monitoring green; continuing telemetry work.
- 2026-03-10 09:15 — Arjun: perf harness updated, need customer traces, blocked on trace redaction.
- 2026-03-11 11:30 — Samir: added dk_fusion_prealloc_bytes to telemetry, dashboard PR open.
- 2026-03-12 08:45 — Dana: CS outreach done for customer A, suggested temporary request-size limits; awaiting customer response.

Appendix: quick snippet of rollback playbook (condensed) — for runbook owners:
- Verify canary health, snapshot canary pool (ASG/VM image)
- If rollback needed: scale canary down to 0% and route traffic to prior revision, escalate pager and post in #incident-release
- Post-rollback checklist: collect core dumps, preserve debug bundle, and open follow-up Jira with prioritization tag

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep hotfix naming convention strict: runtime-kernel v{semver}-hotfix{n} to avoid confusion.
- Perf tests: add a "long tail mixer" traffic generator to simulate 0.5% of requests at 5x seq_len.

-- end of notes --
